items.title: Two claimed proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis in one day
items.explainer: A mathematician at Anthropic says he and Claude proved the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization, and he released the proof as Lean code, a language a computer can check line by line. It is about 1.3GB, roughly 250,000 page equivalents, far too long for a person to read. Hours later a human mathematician released a 940-page draft he had worked on for 12 years.
items.why: This is the clearest example yet of a correct-looking AI result that no human can read, which is exactly the problem teachers have with AI-written student work.

items.title: After the 'mathocalypse,' mathematicians ask what their job is now
items.explainer: An MIT panel looked at a year in which AI agents produced a proof related to Navier-Stokes and OpenAI released 722 manuscripts claiming solved problems. Panelists argued that math needs human understanding, and one journal hired an extra editor to deal with the flood of AI-assisted submissions.
items.why: The same questions about understanding, credit and review are coming to every discipline, music theory included.

items.title: Physics-constrained AI models for chaotic systems
items.explainer: Researchers make AI models obey physical laws while they predict chaotic systems such as weather. The constraint keeps forecasts from drifting into impossible states over long runs.
items.why: It's a concrete example of building rules into a model instead of trusting raw prediction, which is a useful way to frame AI for clients.

tryThisWeek.title: Sort one assignment with the traffic light
tryThisWeek.steps: Choose one assignment and label it red (AI prohibited), yellow (limited supporting use) or green (using AI is the skill). Write one sentence for students explaining why it got that colour, then ask them whether they agree.

hook: If students score near 100% on homework, what do you think they average on the proctored exam?

lead.title: A proof nobody can read
lead.dek: An AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis arrived as 1.3GB of machine-checked code on the same day as a 940-page human draft, so math now has to decide which kind of truth it trusts.
paragraphs: On November 20, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a short note saying that, working with Claude, he believes he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and that the method extends to the generalized version. He did not release a paper. He released Lean code, a formal language whose checker confirms every logical step mechanically.

The release is about 1.3GB, roughly 250,000 page equivalents. The work began on October 6 and the final step landed on November 16. Within hours, Stanford's Ravi Vakil announced a separate, all-human proof of the generalized hypothesis by Alessandro Masullo: a 940-page draft that Brian Conrad has been checking for months.

One newsletter summed it up as a proof that is probably correct but incomprehensible set against one that is probably flawed in places but understandable. If the Lean code compiles with no extra assumptions, the logic holds. What a human then has to confirm is that the formal statement really says what the Riemann Hypothesis says.
lead.against: Neither proof is verified yet, and in September a Lean proof related to Navier-Stokes was criticized for not matching the result it claimed. Experts say both new claims will take years to settle.
lead.watch: Whether the Lean code finishes compiling cleanly, and whether independent number theorists accept that its formal statement matches the hypothesis.
lead.ask: If a student hands in work that is correct but that neither of you can explain, what grade does it deserve?

graph.title: Homework versus the exam
graph.tease: NYU Tandon faculty compared homework scores with proctored exam scores in one foundational course.
graph.question: Homework scores were near 100%. What was the proctored exam average?
graph.reveal: The exam average was about 50%, half the homework score. The NYU guide calls this gap learning loss: correct work handed in without the skill behind it.
graph.caveat: One course, reported by NYU Tandon and quoted in a news summary. The figures are approximate, and the gap does not prove AI caused it.
